newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian parliament unites against racism.
newsitem.headline: Australian parliament unites against racism.

text.p: Australia's government and opposition, stirred by a divisive community debate on racism and immigration, united on Wednesday to condemn racial prejudice.

Facing a mounting backlash from Asia and growing criticism at home over the race row, Prime Minister John Howard accepted a Labor opposition proposal for a joint parliamentary motion condemning racism and pledging a tolerant and open society.

"This motion, it is about saying to the Australian people and saying to the nations of the region that we are a tolerant society, we are a compassionate society..." Howard said in moving the motion, which was carried by an overwhelming majority.
"It is also a statement of some fundamental beliefs about the nature of our existence as human beings in Australia."
Asian newspapers have criticised Howard for failing to take a tough stand against outspoken independent politician Pauline Hanson, who sparked the race debate.

Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said on Wednesday he had written to the Bangkok-based The Nation newspaper rejecting as "inaccurate and offensive" an editorial headlined "Howard's silence endorses Australia's racist fringe".
But Downer conceded that if the row carried on, it could tarnish Australia's image in the region.

Hanson, from conservative northern Queensland state, complained in her maiden parliamentary speech last month that Australia was being swamped by Asians and called for an immediate halt to immigration.

A magazine poll published on Wednesday found two out of three Australians backed her anti-immigration stand and said a Hanson-led political party would easily win an influential bloc of parliamentary seats. Hanson was absent for Wednesday's parliamentary debate.
Her comments have been blamed for a rise in incidents of racial abuse and a sharp increase in official racism complaints to the human rights commission.
"I, for one, haven't been very proud to be an Australian the last few weeks," deputy opposition leader Gareth Evans, a former foreign minister, told parliament.
Howard's conservative Liberal-National government, while condemning racism, has defended Hanson's right to speak out and has blamed the racism controversy on the media.
Howard told parliament Australia, with a large and diverse mix of immigrants, was one of the world's most tolerant nations.

"There are few nations in the world that can boast such a record of democracy, such a record of fair treatment and such a record of harmoniously blending together of people of different racial backgrounds than Australia," he said.
The motion said the lower house "denounces racial intolerance in any form as incompatible with the kind of society we want to be".

It also reaffirms the right of all Australians to be "treated with equal respect regardless of race, colour, creed or origin" and "reaffirms its commmitment to maintaining Australia as a culturally diverse, tolerant and open society".
